Perfect crystals and real crystals

A perfect crystal is an ideal reference in which every lattice site has its prescribed occupant and the periodic arrangement extends without interruption. At any temperature above absolute zero, real crystals contain thermodynamically generated point defects. Additional defects arise during growth, deformation, irradiation and doping.

DimensionalityDefect classExamples
0DPoint defectVacancy, interstitial, substitutional impurity
1DLine defectEdge and screw dislocations
2DPlanar defectGrain boundary, stacking fault, twin boundary
3DVolume defectPore, inclusion, precipitate

The elementary chemistry chapter concentrates on point defects because they directly affect stoichiometry, density, colour and electrical behaviour.

Stoichiometric intrinsic defects

A stoichiometric defect preserves the overall cation:anion ratio of the ideal compound.

DefectMicroscopic eventDensity effectTypical conditions/examples
Vacancy defect in an elemental solidAn atom is absent from a normal siteDecreasesHigh temperature
Interstitial defect in an elemental solidAn extra atom occupies an interstitial siteIncreasesSmall atoms/open structures
Schottky defectEqual stoichiometric numbers of cations and anions are missingDecreasesHigh coordination, similar ion sizes: NaCl, KCl, CsCl
Frenkel defectA smaller ion leaves its site and occupies an interstitial positionApproximately unchangedLarge size difference, lower CN: AgCl, AgBr, ZnS
ρdefective<ρidealfor Schottky disorder\rho_{defective}<\rho_{ideal}\quad\text{for Schottky disorder}ρdefective​<ρideal​for Schottky disorder
ρdefective≈ρidealfor Frenkel disorder\rho_{defective}\approx\rho_{ideal}\quad\text{for Frenkel disorder}ρdefective​≈ρideal​for Frenkel disorder
AgBr can show both

Silver bromide can exhibit both Schottky and Frenkel disorder. Lists of ‘typical examples’ are trends, not exclusive laws.

Thermodynamics of defect formation

Creating a defect costs enthalpy but increases configurational entropy. The equilibrium concentration therefore increases with temperature.

n≈Nexp⁡(−ΔHfkT)n\approx N\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H_f}{kT}\right)n≈Nexp(−kTΔHf​​)

Schematic dependence for independent point defects; exact prefactors and exponents depend on the defect reaction.

Derivation · Schottky-pair scaling
KS∝(nN)2K_S\propto\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)^2KS​∝(Nn​)2

A neutral pair contains one cation vacancy and one anion vacancy.

KS=exp⁡(−ΔGSkT)K_S=\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G_S}{kT}\right)KS​=exp(−kTΔGS​​)

Equilibrium follows the free energy of pair formation.

Result
nN∝exp⁡(−ΔGS2kT)\frac{n}{N}\propto\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G_S}{2kT}\right)Nn​∝exp(−2kTΔGS​​)

JEE questions usually test the qualitative trend: defect concentration rises exponentially with temperature and falls as formation energy increases.

Impurity defects and charge compensation

A substitutional impurity of different charge requires compensation to preserve macroscopic electroneutrality. Compensation can occur through vacancies, interstitials or changes in oxidation state.

1
Worked example

SrCl2_22​ doped NaCl

A crystal contains 10−310^{-3}10−3 mol SrCl2_22​ substitutionally dissolved in 1 mol NaCl. Neglect other defects. How many Na+^++ vacancies are created?

  1. Each Sr2+^{2+}2+ occupies one Na+^++ site but supplies one extra positive charge relative to Na+^++.
  2. One Na+^++ vacancy, carrying one effective negative charge, compensates each Sr2+^{2+}2+ substitution.
  3. Therefore moles of Na vacancies equal moles of SrCl2_22​.
10−310^{-3}10−3 mol of Na+^++ vacancies are created.
SrCl2 in NaCl:[VNa]=[SrNa∙]\mathrm{SrCl_2\ in\ NaCl}:\quad [V_{Na}]=[Sr_{Na}^{\bullet}]SrCl2​ in NaCl:[VNa​]=[SrNa∙​]

Effective-charge notation is shown schematically.

Vacancy count, not missing pairs

One divalent cation replacing a monovalent cation creates one monovalent-cation vacancy per dopant, not one anion vacancy.

Metal-excess defects

A metal-excess solid contains effectively more metal than required by the ideal stoichiometric ratio, usually because negative charge is stored as electrons.

MechanismDescriptionExample/effect
Anion vacancy with trapped electronAn anion leaves; an electron occupies the vacancy to maintain neutrality. The electron-containing vacancy is an F-centre.NaCl heated in Na vapour; yellow colour
Interstitial cation plus electronExtra metal ions enter interstitial sites and electrons occupy nearby interstitial regions or conduction states.ZnO on heating loses O2_22​ and becomes yellow, n-type
OO→12O2(g)+VO∙∙+2e−\mathrm{O_O\rightarrow\tfrac12O_2(g)+V_O^{\bullet\bullet}+2e^-}OO​→21​O2​(g)+VO∙∙​+2e−

F-centres absorb visible light because the trapped electron has quantised states in the vacancy potential. The absorbed wavelength and observed colour depend on the host lattice.

2
Worked example

Stoichiometry of oxygen-deficient ZnO

Write the qualitative formula of zinc oxide after slight oxygen loss.

  1. Oxygen vacancies reduce the oxygen content below one per zinc.
  2. Electrons left behind preserve charge balance and produce n-type conductivity.
The composition is written ZnO1−x\mathrm{ZnO_{1-x}}ZnO1−x​ with x>0x>0x>0.

Metal-deficiency defects

Metal deficiency commonly occurs when a metal can adopt more than one oxidation state. Some lower-valent cation sites are vacant, while other cations oxidise to maintain electroneutrality.

In wüstite, often written Fe1−x_{1-x}1−x​O, some Fe2+^{2+}2+ sites are vacant and a corresponding fraction of Fe2+^{2+}2+ ions becomes Fe3+^{3+}3+.

3
Worked example

Fe0.95_{0.95}0.95​O oxidation-state fraction

Assume oxide is O2−^{2-}2−. In Fe0.95_{0.95}0.95​O, let yyy mol of iron per formula be Fe3+^{3+}3+ and the rest Fe2+^{2+}2+. Find yyy.

  1. Charge balance: 3y+2(0.95−y)=23y+2(0.95-y)=23y+2(0.95−y)=2.
  2. 3y+1.90−2y=23y+1.90-2y=23y+1.90−2y=2.
  3. y=0.10y=0.10y=0.10.
Per Fe0.95_{0.95}0.95​O, 0.10 Fe is Fe3+^{3+}3+ and 0.85 Fe is Fe2+^{2+}2+; about 10.53% of occupied Fe sites are Fe3+^{3+}3+.

Density changes caused by defects

The theoretical density formula can be modified by replacing the ideal cell mass with the actual mass after defects. Cell-volume change is often neglected in elementary problems unless stated.

ρ′=mideal−mmissing+maddedVcell\rho'=\frac{m_{ideal}-m_{missing}+m_{added}}{V_{cell}}ρ′=Vcell​mideal​−mmissing​+madded​​
4
Worked example

Schottky fraction from density

A crystal has ideal density ρ0\rho_0ρ0​ and measured density 0.99ρ00.99\rho_00.99ρ0​. Assume the cell volume is unchanged and only whole formula units are missing through Schottky defects. Estimate the fraction of formula units missing.

  1. Density is proportional to mass per cell when volume is unchanged.
  2. ρ/ρ0=0.99\rho/\rho_0=0.99ρ/ρ0​=0.99 means 99% of ideal mass remains.
  3. Missing fraction is 1%.
Approximately 1% of formula units are absent.

Extended defects and mechanical behaviour

Dislocations allow plastic deformation at stresses far below those required to shear an entire perfect plane simultaneously. Grain boundaries interrupt periodicity and can impede dislocation motion, which is why reducing grain size often strengthens metals.

DefectStructural ideaImportant consequence
Edge dislocationExtra half-plane of atomsPlastic slip
Screw dislocationHelical mismatch around a linePlastic slip and crystal growth
Stacking faultIncorrect local layer sequenceChanges close-packed polytype/local energy
Grain boundaryInterface between orientationsDiffusion path; can strengthen or embrittle
Scope

Detailed dislocation theory is beyond the standard JEE syllabus, but recognising the link between defects and real mechanical properties prevents the false idea that defects are merely imperfections with no function.

Part review

1

Schottky disorder removes stoichiometric ion pairs and lowers density.

2

Frenkel disorder moves an ion to an interstitial site and leaves density nearly unchanged.

3

Aliovalent doping requires charge compensation.

4

F-centres are electrons trapped in anion vacancies.

5

Metal deficiency is commonly balanced by oxidation of some remaining cations.

Practice questions

  1. Compare Schottky and Frenkel defects in a table.
  2. Explain the colour of NaCl heated in sodium vapour.
  3. Calculate the Fe3+^{3+}3+ fraction in Fe0.90_{0.90}0.90​O.
  4. Why does SrCl2_22​ doping create Na+^++ vacancies in NaCl?
  5. Predict the temperature dependence of intrinsic vacancy concentration.

Concept extension Vacancies remove particles from their normal sites. A Frenkel pair moves an ion from its site into an interstice.

Worked example One cation vacancy and one anion vacancy in a 1:1 salt can preserve charge neutrality.

From atomic orbitals to energy bands

When a very large number of atoms forms a solid, each atomic orbital splits into an enormous number of closely spaced crystal orbitals. These levels merge into allowed energy bands separated by forbidden energy gaps.

TermMeaning
Valence bandHighest band occupied at absolute zero in an ordinary semiconductor or insulator
Conduction bandHigher band whose mobile carriers can transport charge
Band gap EgE_gEg​Forbidden energy interval between valence- and conduction-band edges
Fermi level EFE_FEF​Chemical potential for electrons; at 0 K it separates occupied and unoccupied states

Electrical conduction requires both mobile charge carriers and nearby unoccupied states into which they can move under an electric field.

Conductors, semiconductors and insulators

ClassBand pictureTemperature dependence of conductivity
MetalPartially filled band or overlapping bandsUsually decreases as temperature rises because lattice scattering increases
SemiconductorSmall band gap, typically of order electron-volts or lessIncreases strongly with temperature as carriers are generated
InsulatorLarge band gapRemains very low under ordinary conditions
σ=nqμ\sigma=nq\muσ=nqμ

For one carrier type: number density nnn, charge magnitude qqq, mobility μ\muμ.

In a metal, carrier density is already large and temperature mainly changes mobility. In a semiconductor, thermal excitation changes carrier density dramatically, often dominating the mobility decrease.

1
Worked example

Temperature trend

Why does the resistance of a pure semiconductor usually fall on heating while that of a metal rises?

  1. Heating a semiconductor promotes many more electrons across the band gap, increasing carrier density.
  2. Heating a metal mainly increases phonon scattering, reducing mobility.
  3. The dominant effects therefore have opposite signs.
Semiconductor conductivity rises; metallic conductivity usually falls with temperature.

Intrinsic semiconductors

An intrinsic semiconductor is chemically pure in the ideal model. Thermal excitation creates an electron in the conduction band and a corresponding hole in the valence band.

n=p=nin=p=n_in=p=ni​
σi=qni(μe+μh)\sigma_i=q n_i(\mu_e+\mu_h)σi​=qni​(μe​+μh​)
ni∝T3/2exp⁡(−Eg2kT)n_i\propto T^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right)ni​∝T3/2exp(−2kTEg​​)

A hole is not a separate positive particle in vacuum; it is a convenient description of the collective motion of missing valence electrons. Under an electric field, electron and hole currents add to the conventional current.

Fermi level

For a symmetric ideal intrinsic semiconductor, EFE_FEF​ lies near the middle of the gap. Different electron and hole effective masses shift it slightly.

Extrinsic semiconductors

Controlled substitutional doping introduces shallow energy levels and greatly increases carrier density without destroying the crystal lattice.

TypeDopant in Si/GeMajority carrierMinority carrierFermi-level shift
n-typeGroup 15 donor: P, As, SbElectronsHolesToward conduction band
p-typeGroup 13 acceptor: B, Al, GaHolesElectronsToward valence band

In n-type material, donor atoms contribute electrons but become fixed positively charged donor ions after ionisation. The crystal remains electrically neutral overall. Similarly, ionised acceptors are fixed negative centres in p-type material.

n-type is not negatively charged

The labels n and p identify the majority mobile carrier. They do not mean the bulk solid carries net negative or positive charge.

2
Worked example

Dopant choice

Which dopant converts silicon into p-type material: phosphorus or boron? Explain.

  1. Silicon has four valence electrons.
  2. Boron has three and leaves one unsatisfied bond that acts as an acceptor level.
  3. Thermal excitation fills the acceptor and leaves a mobile hole.
Boron produces p-type silicon.

The p–n junction

When p-type and n-type regions meet, majority carriers diffuse across the interface and recombine. Fixed ionised donors and acceptors remain, creating a depletion region and an internal electric field that opposes further diffusion.

BiasEffect on barrier/depletion widthCurrent
Forward biasReduces barrier and narrows depletion regionLarge majority-carrier current
Reverse biasRaises effective barrier and widens depletion regionSmall minority-carrier current until breakdown

Rectification follows because the junction conducts much more readily in forward bias than in reverse bias. Light can generate electron–hole pairs, enabling photodiodes and solar cells.

3
Worked example

Forward-bias identification

For a silicon diode, which terminal should be connected to the p side for forward bias?

  1. Forward bias must lower the junction barrier.
  2. Connect the p region to the positive terminal and the n region to the negative terminal.
Positive to p and negative to n gives forward bias.

Ionic and mixed conduction

In ionic solids, charge can be transported by ions moving through vacancies or interstitial pathways. Ionic conductivity therefore depends strongly on defect concentration, migration energy and temperature.

σion∝ndefectexp⁡(−EmkT)\sigma_{ion}\propto n_{defect}\exp\left(-\frac{E_m}{kT}\right)σion​∝ndefect​exp(−kTEm​​)

Fast-ion conductors such as stabilised zirconia, beta-alumina and some fluorite oxides have connected pathways and abundant mobile defects. Some materials conduct both ions and electrons and are called mixed conductors.

Solid ionic conductors exist

The elementary rule ‘ionic solids do not conduct’ means ordinary defect-poor crystals conduct poorly at room temperature. It is not an absolute statement for all solids and temperatures.

Superconductivity

A superconductor below its critical temperature exhibits zero dc electrical resistance and expels magnetic flux from its interior, the Meissner effect. Perfect conductivity alone does not define superconductivity; magnetic flux expulsion is essential.

QuantityMeaning
Critical temperature TcT_cTc​Highest temperature for the superconducting state at specified field/current
Critical field HcH_cHc​ or Hc1,Hc2H_{c1},H_{c2}Hc1​,Hc2​Magnetic-field limits of the superconducting state
Critical current density JcJ_cJc​Current-density limit before superconductivity is destroyed
Meissner effectExpulsion of magnetic flux on cooling through TcT_cTc​

Type I superconductors show one critical field and complete flux exclusion below it. Type II superconductors have a mixed vortex state between lower and upper critical fields and are more useful in high-field magnets.

BCS and high-TcT_cTc​ materials

Conventional superconductors are described by Cooper pairing mediated by lattice vibrations. Cuprate high-TcT_cTc​ superconductors are more complex; detailed microscopic theory is outside the JEE syllabus.

Numerical relations and diagnostic plots

4
Worked example

Intrinsic carrier ratio

Two intrinsic semiconductors at the same temperature have gaps 1.0 eV and 1.4 eV. Ignoring prefactors, find the ratio ni,1/ni,2n_{i,1}/n_{i,2}ni,1​/ni,2​ at 300 K, where kT≈0.0259kT\approx0.0259kT≈0.0259 eV.

  1. ni∝exp⁡[−Eg/(2kT)]n_i\propto\exp[-E_g/(2kT)]ni​∝exp[−Eg​/(2kT)].
  2. Ratio =exp⁡[(1.4−1.0)/(2×0.0259)]=\exp[(1.4-1.0)/(2\times0.0259)]=exp[(1.4−1.0)/(2×0.0259)].
  3. Exponent ≈7.72\approx7.72≈7.72, so ratio ≈2.25×103\approx2.25\times10^3≈2.25×103.
The smaller-gap semiconductor has roughly 2.3×1032.3\times10^32.3×103 times the intrinsic carrier density.

A plot of ln⁡σ\ln\sigmalnσ or ln⁡ni\ln n_ilnni​ against 1/T1/T1/T is approximately linear in an activated regime. The slope can be used to estimate an activation energy or half the band gap, depending on the measured quantity and assumptions.

Fermi–Dirac occupancy

The probability that an available one-electron state of energy EEE is occupied at temperature TTT is given by the Fermi–Dirac distribution.

f(E)=11+exp⁡[(E−EF)/(kT)]f(E)=\frac{1}{1+\exp[(E-E_F)/(kT)]}f(E)=1+exp[(E−EF​)/(kT)]1​
  • At E=EFE=E_FE=EF​, f=1/2f=1/2f=1/2 at every non-zero temperature.
  • At 0 K, states below EFE_FEF​ are occupied and those above are empty.
  • Thermal broadening occurs over an energy scale of order kTkTkT.
Band occupancy is not carrier density by itself

Carrier concentration also depends on the density of available states. The Fermi function supplies the occupation probability.

Purification and liquid-crystal materials

Semiconductor devices require extremely pure material. In zone refining, a narrow molten zone moves along a solid bar. When an impurity has distribution coefficient k=Csolid/Cliquid<1k=C_{solid}/C_{liquid}<1k=Csolid​/Cliquid​<1, it prefers the melt and is swept toward one end through repeated passes.

Liquid crystals combine fluidity with orientational order. Nematic phases possess average molecular alignment without layered positional order; smectic phases possess layers; cholesteric phases show a helical director. Their optical anisotropy can be controlled by electric fields.

PhaseOrientational orderLayering
NematicYesNo
SmecticYesYes
CholestericLocally nematic with helical twistNo simple equally spaced layers required
LCD principle

A twisted-nematic display uses field-controlled molecular orientation to change the polarisation state and transmitted intensity of light between polarisers.

Part review

1

Bands arise from splitting of atomic levels in a periodic solid.

2

Metals have available nearby states; semiconductors have a small gap; insulators a large gap.

3

Intrinsic semiconductors satisfy n=pn=pn=p.

4

Donors create n-type and acceptors p-type material without net bulk charge.

5

Superconductivity requires zero resistance and the Meissner effect.

  1. Explain why a filled valence band cannot conduct by itself.
  2. Derive the intrinsic conductivity expression.
  3. Distinguish majority carriers, minority carriers and fixed dopant ions.
  4. Sketch how forward bias changes a p–n junction depletion region.
  5. Why is zero resistance alone insufficient to define a superconductor?

Origin of magnetic moments

Magnetism arises mainly from electron orbital motion and electron spin. In many transition-metal and lanthanide compounds, partially filled shells carry permanent moments. In closed-shell species, applied fields induce small opposing currents that produce diamagnetism.

μ=−gμBJℏ\boldsymbol{\mu}= -g\mu_B\frac{\mathbf{J}}{\hbar}μ=−gμB​ℏJ​

For many first-row transition-metal ions in complexes where orbital angular momentum is substantially quenched, the spin-only approximation is useful.

μso=n(n+2) μB\mu_{so}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mu_Bμso​=n(n+2)​μB​

nnn is the number of unpaired electrons.

1
Worked example

Spin-only moment

Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of a high-spin d5d^5d5 ion.

  1. A high-spin d5d^5d5 ion has five unpaired electrons.
  2. μ=5(5+2)μB=35μB\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}\mu_B=\sqrt{35}\mu_Bμ=5(5+2)​μB​=35​μB​.
μ≈5.92 μB\mu\approx5.92\,\mu_Bμ≈5.92μB​.

Magnetic field quantities and susceptibility

Magnetisation MMM is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume. In a linear material, it is proportional to applied magnetic field strength HHH.

M=χHM=\chi HM=χH
B=μ0(H+M)=μ0(1+χ)HB=\mu_0(H+M)=\mu_0(1+\chi)HB=μ0​(H+M)=μ0​(1+χ)H
ResponseSign/magnitude of χ\chiχField behaviour
DiamagneticSmall negativeWeakly repelled; induced moment opposes field
ParamagneticSmall positiveWeakly attracted; permanent moments partially align
FerromagneticVery large positive below TCT_CTC​Spontaneous magnetisation and domains
AntiferromagneticOrdered opposing moments below TNT_NTN​Net moment ideally zero
FerrimagneticOpposing unequal sublattice momentsNon-zero spontaneous magnetisation
All matter is diamagnetic at some level

Paramagnetism or cooperative ordering usually dominates when unpaired electrons are present. Diamagnetism remains as a smaller background contribution.

Diamagnetism and paramagnetism

Diamagnetic substances contain no required permanent net moment in zero field and develop an induced moment opposite to the applied field. Their susceptibility is nearly temperature independent. Paramagnets contain permanent moments that are randomly oriented without a field and partially align when a field is applied.

χ=CT\chi=\frac{C}{T}χ=TC​

Curie's law for an ideal paramagnet.

μeff=2.828χMT μB\mu_{eff}=2.828\sqrt{\chi_MT}\,\mu_Bμeff​=2.828χM​T​μB​

Common cgs relation when molar susceptibility is in cm3 mol−1\mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}cm3mol−1.

ClassExamples
DiamagneticNaCl, ZnO with Zn2+^{2+}2+ d10d^{10}d10, H2_22​O, diamond
ParamagneticO2_22​, Fe3+^{3+}3+ salts, Cu2+^{2+}2+ salts, many transition-metal ions
2
Worked example

Unpaired electrons from moment

A compound has a spin-only moment close to 3.87 μB3.87\,\mu_B3.87μB​. Estimate the number of unpaired electrons.

  1. Compare with n(n+2)\sqrt{n(n+2)}n(n+2)​.
  2. For n=3n=3n=3, 15=3.87\sqrt{15}=3.8715​=3.87.
The ion has three unpaired electrons.

Ferromagnetism and domains

In a ferromagnet, exchange interactions favour parallel alignment of neighbouring moments below the Curie temperature TCT_CTC​. A macroscopic specimen divides into domains to reduce magnetostatic energy. In an unmagnetised sample, domain magnetisations can cancel even though each domain is internally ordered.

An applied field moves domain walls and rotates domain moments. After the field is removed, some magnetisation can remain, producing hysteresis.

Hysteresis termMeaningMaterial implication
SaturationAll accessible domains alignedMaximum magnetisation
RemanenceMagnetisation at zero field after saturationHigh for permanent magnets
Coercive fieldReverse field required to reduce MMM to zeroLow for transformer cores; high for permanent magnets
Loop areaEnergy dissipated per magnetic cycleSmall for soft magnetic materials

Above TCT_CTC​, thermal disorder destroys long-range ferromagnetic order and the material becomes paramagnetic, often following a Curie–Weiss law.

χ=CT−θ\chi=\frac{C}{T-\theta}χ=T−θC​

For a ferromagnet, θ\thetaθ is generally positive and close to TCT_CTC​.

3
Worked example

Soft versus hard magnet

Which material is preferred for a transformer core: one with a narrow or wide hysteresis loop?

  1. The core is magnetised and demagnetised every ac cycle.
  2. Energy loss per cycle equals the loop area.
  3. A narrow loop also implies low coercivity.
A soft magnetic material with a narrow hysteresis loop is preferred.

Antiferromagnetism and ferrimagnetism

In an antiferromagnet, neighbouring sublattice moments align antiparallel with equal magnitude, giving zero ideal net magnetisation below the Néel temperature TNT_NTN​. In a ferrimagnet, sublattice moments are antiparallel but unequal, so a net moment remains.

OrderSublattice relationNet momentExamples
FerromagneticParallelLargeFe, Co, Ni
AntiferromagneticAntiparallel and equalIdeally zeroMnO, NiO, Cr2_22​O3_33​
FerrimagneticAntiparallel and unequalNon-zeroFe3_33​O4_44​, ferrites MFe2_22​O4_44​

In magnetite, Fe3+^{3+}3+ moments on tetrahedral and octahedral sites largely cancel, while Fe2+^{2+}2+ moments on octahedral sites produce the net ferrimagnetic moment in the simplified ionic picture.

Paramagnetic does not mean non-interacting forever

A material can be paramagnetic above an ordering temperature and become ferro-, antiferro- or ferrimagnetic below it.

Temperature laws and magnetic ordering

RegimeTypical relationInterpretation
Ideal paramagnetχ=C/T\chi=C/Tχ=C/TIndependent moments
Curie–Weiss paramagnetχ=C/(T−θ)\chi=C/(T-\theta)χ=C/(T−θ)Mean-field interactions
Ferromagnet above TCT_CTC​θ>0\theta>0θ>0Predominantly parallel correlations
Antiferromagnet above TNT_NTN​Often θ<0\theta<0θ<0Predominantly antiparallel correlations

Curie-law comparison

  1. M=χH=(C/T)HM=\chi H=(C/T)HM=χH=(C/T)H.
  2. Doubling TTT halves MMM at fixed HHH.
M2=M1/2M_2=M_1/2M2​=M1​/2.

For isolated first-row transition-metal ions, count unpaired d electrons after considering oxidation state and, where relevant, ligand-field splitting. In solids, exchange coupling can then create cooperative order.

Ion/configurationUnpaired electrons in common high-spin caseSpin-only moment

Spin-only limitations

Co2+^{2+}2+ and many heavier ions can show substantial orbital contributions. Lanthanide moments generally require the full LLL, SSS, JJJ treatment rather than simple unpaired-electron counting.

Critical fields and magnetic measurement

For an ideal Type I superconductor, a commonly used empirical temperature dependence of the thermodynamic critical field is

Hc(T)=Hc(0)[1−(TTc)2]H_c(T)=H_c(0)\left[1-\left(\frac{T}{T_c}\right)^2\right]Hc​(T)=Hc​(0)[1−(Tc​T​)2]

Type II superconductors instead possess lower and upper critical fields Hc1H_{c1}Hc1​ and Hc2H_{c2}Hc2​, with quantised vortices in the mixed state between them.

MethodWhat it measures
Gouy balanceForce on a sample in a non-uniform magnetic field; used to estimate susceptibility
Faraday balanceMagnetic force on a small sample in a field gradient
SQUID magnetometerExtremely sensitive magnetic flux and moment using superconducting quantum interference
Measurement sign

Diamagnetic samples are driven toward weaker field; paramagnetic samples toward stronger field in a field gradient.

Concept extension Classify magnetic order by moment alignment and net response.

Worked example Equal opposite sublattice moments cancel in an ideal antiferromagnet. Unequal opposite moments give ferrimagnetism.

Polarization and dielectric response

A dielectric is an electrical insulator that polarizes in an applied field. Electronic polarization shifts electron clouds relative to nuclei; ionic polarization shifts oppositely charged ions; orientational polarization turns permanent dipoles. The relative permittivity εr measures how strongly the material reduces the field compared with vacuum.

In a simple linear isotropic medium, P = ε0χeE and εr = 1 + χe. These relations do not describe all ferroelectric materials, whose polarization can depend on field history and domain switching.

Example. If χe = 3, then εr = 4. Inserting the dielectric between capacitor plates increases the ideal capacitance by a factor of four when geometry stays fixed.

Concept extension An applied electric field can induce electronic or ionic displacement and orient existing dipoles.

Worked example In a parallel-plate capacitor fully filled with a linear dielectric, C = εᵣC₀.

Practice What happens to capacitance when εᵣ = 4 at fixed geometry?

Show answer

It quadruples.

Thermal and pressure-driven changes

Heating usually expands a crystal lattice, although some materials have unusual directional or negative thermal expansion. For a small temperature interval, a(T) ≈ a0[1 + αΔT], where α is the linear thermal-expansion coefficient. For an isotropic cubic crystal, V(T) ≈ V0[1 + 3αΔT] to first order.

Pressure tends to favour denser structures, but the actual phase depends on free energy, bonding and temperature. A structural phase transition may change symmetry, coordination number or unit-cell dimensions. Do not infer a new structure from pressure alone without phase data.

Example. If a0 = 400 pm, α = 10−5 K−1 and ΔT = 100 K, then a ≈ 400.4 pm.

Concept extension Phase stability depends on temperature and pressure through Gibbs free energy. Pressure tends to favour the lower-volume phase.

Worked example At a given temperature the pressure term favours a denser polymorph if other contributions permit a transition.

Practice Can pressure change crystal structure at fixed composition?

Semiconductor and defect chemistry

Worked example

Radius ratio and pressure

A salt changes from NaCl-type to CsCl-type under high pressure. Explain the coordination change.

  1. NaCl type has CN 6; CsCl type has CN 8.
  2. High pressure favours structures with higher coordination and often higher density.
  3. The rigid ambient-pressure radius-ratio chart cannot alone describe compressed ions.
Pressure stabilises the denser 8-coordinate CsCl-type arrangement.

Revision strategy

For any numerical problem, first identify the structural model and write one geometrical relation, one counting relation and one physical-property relation. Most difficult-looking questions reduce to a controlled combination of these three.

Practice At fixed molar mass, what happens if an FCC material’s edge increases by 1%?

Show answer

Density falls by about 3%, assuming the same occupancy.

FINAL APPENDIX

Optional appendix: Miller indices and lattice planes

Miller indices and interplanar spacing

Miller indices encode the orientation of a family of parallel lattice planes. Find the intercepts of a plane on the a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c axes in lattice units, take reciprocals, and clear fractions. An infinite intercept gives reciprocal zero; a negative intercept is written with a bar.

  • Intercepts (a,∞,∞)(a,\infty,\infty)(a,∞,∞) give (100)(100)(100).
  • Intercepts (a,b,∞)(a,b,\infty)(a,b,∞) give (110)(110)(110).
  • Intercepts (a,b,c)(a,b,c)(a,b,c) give (111)(111)(111).
  • A plane through the origin is replaced by a parallel plane before taking intercepts.
Derivation · Cubic interplanar spacing
∣Ghkl∣=2πah2+k2+l2|\mathbf G_{hkl}|=\frac{2\pi}{a}\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}∣Ghkl​∣=a2π​h2+k2+l2​

The reciprocal-lattice vector is normal to the (hkl)(hkl)(hkl) planes.

dhkl=2π∣Ghkl∣d_{hkl}=\frac{2\pi}{|\mathbf G_{hkl}|}dhkl​=∣Ghkl​∣2π​

Adjacent planes differ in phase by one full reciprocal period.

Result

Interactive explanation

Build a Miller plane

Find the intercepts of a plane with the crystallographic axes, divide by a, take reciprocals, then reduce to the smallest integers. A parallel axis has an infinite intercept and therefore index 0.

Where these indices are used

  • Unit cell geometry: identify the orientation of a slice through a crystal.
  • X-ray diffraction and Bragg’s law: label the parallel planes associated with a reflection. For a cubic cell, dₕₖₗ = a/√(h² + k² + l²). For example, d₁₁₀ = a/√2.
  • Close packing: the close-packed layers in FCC are parallel to planes of the {111} family.

Parentheses, such as (111), identify a plane orientation; braces, such as {111}, group symmetry-equivalent orientations. A bar indicates a negative index. Square brackets identify a direction.

For example, intercepts a/2, a and ∞ in a cubic cell give normalized intercepts ½, 1 and ∞. Taking reciprocals gives (210). If a plane passes through the origin, use a parallel representative that avoids it to read its orientation.
